EDF is one of the most entrancing yet mystifying series in all of video games. A mechanical analysis of the game would center around its most prominent 'flaws': 
- 80 missions with no coherent context, featuring similar city-scape sandboxes and nonsensical underground burrows
- Glitchy physics where giant bugs are propelled across the sky by your explosive weapons
- Hundreds of unlockable weapons and vehicles, many of which are broken to the point of being useless 
- Voice tracks of screaming soldiers and moronic scientists that have no correlation to what's happening on screen 
An analysis of systems and function would pronounce this game a dismal failure, and leave it there. 

But only someone with no joy in their soul could miss the forrest for the trees and misdiagnose this game as anything other than a spectacular success. Every glitchy giant ant that you propel into the stratosphere is cause for mad giggling. Every weapon unlock is a thrilling lottery - you might find an orbital ion cannon painter that vaporises swarms of bugs, or you might be gifted a hilariously useless assault rifle that sprays two lines in a horizontal V pattern. Your vehicle unlock could be a colossal megazord mech that punches the freak out of elastic Michelin man alien robots, or it could be a motorbike with a side-car featuring the worst turning of anything ever coded. But in the spirit of mad experimentation, you'll jump into it anyway with your friends, and barrel into swarms of hopping tarantulas, cackling like maniacs. 

Somehow you'll survive, with the city you've been entrusted to save now just flattened rubble. All civilians massacred. Your commanders over radio will declare your mission an unqualified triumph, and you will be whisked off to your next mission. Alien orb motherships loom ominously in the sky, dropships spew streams of ants, moronic attack drone swarms bumble and richochet off buildings as they attempt to strafe you with lazer globs. But you will hang your head high, knowing that you have nothing to fear. You are the EDF - the finest Earth has to offer against the alien menace. And you will emerge victorious.

Collect new weapons and increase armor across four classes while stomping alien invaders and their bug friends to bits, the only good bug is a dead bug. Each armor pickup gives your class chosen a small bit of armor for the next time you use them. Each weapon pickup has a random chance at one of hundreds of weapons per class you were when you picked it up.  The game allows multiple playthrough by offering harder, faster, stronger enemies as the difficulty is increased, not only by playing later missions but also a selectable difficulty option per each mission.  After obtaining more powerful weapons and increasing armor, you can then take on those harder settings. On those hard difficulties comes higher loot tables for better weapons. Across over more than 80 levels, there is a lot to see and even more to do.

With each player class playing different than the next, you are guaranteed to find one that suits you and your playstyle. 

- An all around Ranger with assault rifles, missles, rockets, shot guns and snipers to name a few. A decent all around character. Has evasive rolls and decent armor. Can select two weapons for a sortie.

- A vehicle summoning and air strike calling support infantry Air Raider. Has building sized vehicles, or small tunnel crawling vehicles. Has health fountain support to heal allies and missile guidance support to help kill.  Has claymors, mines and auto turrets. Harder to play than a Ranger, but rewarding and unique. Same evasive rolls and same decent armor as the ranger. Can select two weapons/support at once and one vehicle for a sortie.

- A guerilla type high-damage dealing Wing Diver. Using a jet pack and constantly recovering energy supply. You fly in, while managing your energy, deal massive damage and back off to recover. Weapons also use this energy, when you over use it your jet pack fails and weapons can no longer reload until your energy system cools off. Very light armor means certain death when you run out of juice in bug city. Can select two weapons for a sortie.

- A Fencer. A high armored walking vehicle-like humanoid suit. Can use incredibly large weapons. Hammers, spears, swords, shields, artillery, missles, etc. Can select two sets of two weapons at once, capable of switching between each set on the fly. The fencer has a jump boost or forward boost depending on his equipped weapon and his armor is unmatched.

The opposition ranges from acid spewing black ants. to tough armored red ants that grab you. To flying alien spaceships and wasps. To giant walking robots and walkers. There are plenty more but I won't spoil any of that. Plenty of variety in alien and bug opposition, to keep you always changing your loadout and tactics.

There isn't much more to say.

Here is a game that brings forth the campy low budget atmosphere of a B-movie into the video gaming world.  All of the above is true:  The graphics, sound, voice acting, plot and gameplay are all pretty meh across the board.  That said, this is perhaps one of the most amusing games third person shooters I've played in many many years.

It helps that the game doesn't take itself too seriously.  While not going full Goat Simulator and relying on 'lol random' to make up for effort on their part, the game designers instead have made almost every level* a sandbox for you to fight giant bugs using progressively more ludicrously overpowered weaponry.  You will go from rocket launchers that take several shots to level a single building to multi-launch missile systems that can level an entire city block with a single squeeze of the trigger.

It's that progression of power in your weaponry that is part of what makes this game so compelling.  The power progression combined with a menace largely composed of big creepy crawlies makes for a video game equivalent of going after an ant hill with a magnifying glass on a sunny day.  Each city level with the bugs has them crawling all over the sky scrapers like they own the place.  And it's oddly satisfying to level said sky scrapers while happily scouring the city of the infestation.  Sure you probably caused more property damage and loss of life than the aliens ever would but /dammit/ if you didn't show those jerks what for!!

We've not even gotten onto the vehicles yet either!  While they're largely limited to a single class (Air Raider), they are pretty cool and include the relatively mundane in helicopters and tanks before going to railgun platforms, mini-mechas, multi-pilot regular mechas, and finally a Jaeger.  Also provided:  A giant Godzilla-alike with the serial numbers filed off for you to punch around in said Jaeger.  Sadly the Jaegers are multi-pilot so no drifting for you but as mentioned above several of the vehicles are multi-pilot and it's pretty cool if you have some buddies to work together with to pilot a tank that is wider across than a four lane highway.

So the Air Raiders have some pretty cool stuff, so maybe you think they're the only class you really need.  But wait!  Why summon in a giant mecha when you can basically be a human-sized mecha as a Fencer?  Sure you're slow as molasses but with the right skill and weaponry you can put out as much if not more damage than anyone else.

Want more mobility?  Try a Wing Diver!  Fragile but with a jetpack that allows unparalleled mobility and a selection of unique laser and plasma based weaponry you can happily glass your foes from above!  At least until the bees arrive.  OH GOD THE BEES.

Want to be boring?  Pick a Ranger!  OK OK I kid.  The Ranger actually is a good balance of mobility and power when compared to the Fencer and Wing Diver.  Sure they can't fly but they have the fastest on foot speed, and their weaponry is simple and effective unlike the unwieldy battleship cannons the Fencer uses or the also-uses-your-jetpack-fuel plasma weaponry of the Wing Diver.

So you have four different ways to fight, but what about things to fight?  Well I've mentioned some examples above but there are many more.  Your enemy will not just employ giant bugs but also various mechanical foes like mechas and flying drones.  Thought the bees were bad?  Try dragons!  You also have huge ships that act as spawners and interlocking plates that will cover the sky overhead.  All of this adds to the challenge as the game goes on and gives you new ways to try and use that arsenal you are trying to stockpile.  Go ahead, call in a nuke on a beach full of giant angry red ants.  It's great fun!

So in conclusion, Earth Defense Force 4.1: The Shadow of New Despair is a great game.  It's not perfect.  It has a ton of flaws thanks to the fact it is a low budget game designed for consoles.  That said I'm excited about the idea of there being a sequel to this game in ways I would never be for other shooters with multi-million dollar budgets.  It's simple, it's enjoyable, and I think it reminds us that that is all you need in the end.  This, to me, is the blueprint that other looter shooters should follow.  Where instead of incremental upgrades of rifle you're waiting to pick up the next ridiculous multi-grenade launcher that can blow up everything around you (and you) in a satisfyingly hilarious way.

If I can make one small suggestion though ... the fact weapon pickups can be duplicates which you get no benefit for it annoying.  At least make them count as armor upgrades or something, SHEESH!!

When talking about Earth Defense Force it’s always worth bringing up how this series came to be. In Japan there exists a long running series of budget-priced video games called the Simple series. These are games made on shoestring budgets by small developers and released at budget prices. There are hundreds of them, the majority of which were never released outside of Japan. Some of these games became popular enough to become their own series, others are just anomalies that are fun for a short while for their absurdity, and others are just shovelware. It’s possible that some of you out there may have played some of them, moreso if you live in PAL territories which saw releases of a bunch of PS2 Simple series games. Earth Defense Force started as a random game in this series and is now arguably the most popular and well-known game in the Simple series.

Earth Defense Force games are often described as being “so bad they’re good” but this description has never sat right with me as it implies that the games are of such low quality that they can only be enjoyed ironically, which is far from the case with these games.
EDF 4.1 is an enhanced version of EDF 2025. The story of the game is as follows; it’s the year 2025 and the world is under attack by giant insects, aliens, and other such nasties. You play as a member of the Earth Defense Force and fight back against the invaders. That’s it. Though you do get updates on the progress of the invasion radioed to you by your superiors as you progress through missions, the game doesn’t take control away from you to force you to watch cutscenes. Make no mistake, this game is fully aware of what you are playing it for - to kill hordes of oversized enemies with ridiculous weapons. You have four classes to pick from (which you can change at any time); Ranger, Air Raider, Wing Diver, and Fencer. Each has their own playstyle, strengths, weaknesses, and weaponry that they specialise in, from the Wing Diver’s jetpack and energy based weapons, to the Air Raider’s ability to call in orbital strikes and pilotable vehicles.

The action is viewed from a third-person perspective as you control your member of the EDF. 
One thing that will immediately stick out once you start playing is that the graphics look quite dated. The developers have always been smart enough to use this to their advantage as it means that each mission can take place in massive levels with destructible environments populated with countless enemies. Mission structure is quite simple - kill anything that moves. Within missions you can recruit other squads of EDF troops to fight with you simply by moving close to them but you’ll be doing most of the heavy lifting… and probably killing your newly recruited allies through friendly fire. Enemies you kill will have a chance to drop health packs, as well as armour and weapon crates. Upon completing a mission the armour crates you gather will increase your maximum health and weapon crates will grant you new weapons (of which there are over 800), which helps on later missions as well as when playing at higher difficulties.
This game has no unnecessary bloat. No arbitrary failure conditions in missions, no out of place crafting to acquire weapons. You can do more damage to the city than the enemies do, but as long as you complete the mission without dying it’s still mission complete, and once you unlock a weapon out of a crate it’s yours forever. This series has always put fun before everything else.

I haven’t even talked about online co-op yet. Like many games, since you’ll be doing pretty much the same thing from start to finish it's likely to get tedious when playing solo. Online co-op will help alleviate this. It might take some effort to convince a few of your friends to play a game with graphics that looked a generation old even when this game originally launched around three weeks after The Last of Us did in 2013, but after they play a few missions they won’t be able to stop themselves from chanting “EDF!” as they charge into battle with you.

[h3]Which EDF game should I buy?[/h3]
Before I start my review in earnest, I’ll try to answer the two most common questions I see regarding which game in this series to purchase:

EDF 4.1 is a remastered version of EDF 2025 that adds some QoL changes, new vehicles and weapons, and new + adjusted enemies. Do not purchase both; get this one instead. If you already have 2025, get something else like 5 or a spinoff or Iron Rain unless you are a hardcore series fan and want to see the very minor amount of extra content that was added/play 2025 with some QoL changes.

EDF 5 is a series reboot; you don’t need to play EDF 4.1 to understand the story or lore of that game and the stories of these games are background excuse plot in the first place anyways. EDF 5 has better graphics and very significant QoL changes; while I haven’t played it to compare myself, my impression is that it’s the better game and that if you can pick only one, you should get EDF 5.

Moving on to the review in earnest:

[h3]What is EDF 4.1?[/h3]
EDF 4.1 is a third-person shooter focused on spectacle and player power fantasy. The player controls a soldier employed by the Earth Defense Force and fights against the forces of the Ravagers, robot aliens and the giant bugs that serve them in their invasion of Earth, in a campaign made of 89 different selectable missions with scripted enemy presence, setpieces, dialogue, and maps. Missions take place on one of 16 unique maps with near-completely destructible cities. These missions come in five difficulties ranging from Easy to Inferno; difficulty modifiers are principally increased damage and health for enemies, along with more friendly fire damage for yourself and allies, but on Hard and then again on Hardest new enemies and new enemy variants will be added to some levels. Missions can be played solo, with a splitscreen partner, or through online multiplayer, the latter of which buffs enemy HP and sometimes damage for each additional player.

The player’s soldier belongs to one of four possible classes: Rangers (flexible infantry with a dodgeroll and wide weapon selection), Wing Divers (flying troops with an energy management system and low survivability), Air Raider (support-centric class that calls in artillery strikes/bombing runs/giant space lasers/etc, vehicles, and turrets), or Fencer (power-armored infantry with immense stopping power and fantastic speed balanced out by their turning/aiming/weapon readying sluggishness). To think of things in standard terms, a player has one character of each class, and selects which character they want to use in a mission. Each character/class upgrades independently; health upgrades and new weapons earned in a mission only apply to the character you played with. Most classes can equip two weapons; Air Raider can take two plus a vehicle and Fencer is allowed two sets of two (four weapons total, but you set them up as pairs that you dual-wield and have to switch both out/in together). You obtain new weapons and permanent health upgrades by picking up loot that defeated enemies have a chance to drop. Ammo is unlimited for most weapons but clip size is not.

Missions mostly revolve around destroying all enemies present and repeating that as new scripted or summoned waves of foes enter the fight until the mission is completed. Combat in this game has a heavy focus on target management and priority, appropriate weapon selection, and player positioning. This is because, overwhelmingly, your opponents are hordes of giant alien insects or alien robots which will either grab and bite you or attack with some kind of relatively short ranged projectile. Individually weak both offensively and health-wise, they rely on sheer numbers to swarm and overwhelm players. And I do mean “sheer numbers” and “hordes” in the most extreme possible sense. Graphical fidelity has been sacrificed to fit as many enemies as possible on screen; they will come at you by the hundreds, to the point where in some levels you can block routes for the enemy by killing so many that their piled-up corpses get the ones behind them stuck.  It is hard to overstate just how integral the concept of swarms is to EDF 4.1.

The game’s story and lore is an afterthought excuse-plot for you to shoot, spear, laser, and explode your way through hordes and hordes of giant alien bugs. It’s like somebody threw every Hollywood B movie into a pot and stirred, complete with incredibly hammy voice acting, gaping plot holes everywhere, and such outstanding dialogue such as “Fiah the REQUIEUM GUUUHN!!!!” It isn’t taking itself seriously and it works pretty well because of it; don’t buy this game if you’re looking for a deep, engrossing story or well-developed characters.

[h3]The Good:[/h3]
[b]Weapon Variety[/b]
This game has a very wide variety of weapons unique in both design and playstyle. Each of the four classes, which themselves play very differently, has a wide range of weapon archetypes (snipers, machineguns, rocket launchers, missile launchers, as examples), and then within those weapon archetypes different types of weapons (for instance, under the category of “artillery” you might have giant single-shot guns, man-portable mortars, giant grapeshot guns, and semiautomatic hand cannons, all of which play fairly differently and are used in different situations). These weapons are generally well balanced and satisfying to use; enemies react to being shot or hit with explosions, recoil and aim-lag are used to make very heavy weapons feel that they have a sense of weight, missiles have very satisfying sound and visual design as they lock onto enemies, explosions send corpses and parts of corpses flying, etc.

[b]Enemy Variety[/b]
Speaking of enemies, there are 7 types of swarm-based enemies, 4 elite or single-target enemies, 4 miniboss-like enemies, 4 boss-like enemies, 3 types of infinite-enemy spawners, and a few miscellaneous things like turrets or forcefield generators lurking in the periphery. While this may seem low on paper, good mission pacing, the use of variants of those enemies (ranging from stat-boosted palate swaps to fundamental changes to necessary approach and battlefield role), and carefully considered enemy placement for each level prevent things from wearing out their welcome. It helps also that the game paces itself somewhat and saves a few novel enemies for its second half.

[b]Large Maps with Fully Destructible Buildings[/b]
The game’s maps are also fairly varied; there are 16 of them and they’re reused with fairly significant variation. The maps are very large (a square kilometer or so) and you will start from and move to different areas in them mission to mission, have certain buildings destroyed or routes blocked/opened, etc. While the city sections can start to feel a little overdone towards the end of the game, the effect generally isn’t too noticeable.

[h3]The Bad:[/h3]
[b]Health Upgrading Grind:[/b]
Upping your health is a pain in the ass. You get 0.212-0.53 points of permanent health increase for each box of armor you pick up, which are uncommonly dropped (and usually one at a time) by defeated enemies. Your character starts with about 200 HP. To just be able to play ball on some missions’ higher difficulties, you may need [i]several thousand[/i] HP depending on your class and available weapons. And you have to do this individually for each class you want to play. That’s a [i]lot[/i] of boxes. You have to constantly be scouring the map for enemy loot, breaking immersion and interrupting the flow of gameplay, and frequently the best strategy is to just leave one relatively weak enemy alive while you waste 5 minutes at the end of each mission picking up all the drops. It’s boring and lame.

There are two series of games that have instantly enthralled me with their character. Those series are [i]Monster Hunter[/i] and [i]EDF[/i]

Now I know what you must be thinking:
"This game is $50 and it's how old? What a rip off! I could get so many tendies with that kind of money!"

I know, I thought the same thing. But a few hours of gameplay in and a few nights without tendies taught me that an old game can actually still be worth $50.

[h1]Performance [/h1]
With most PC games you can usually run a game with minimal issues even if you don't meet the minimum requirements.
[b]Not with this game you can't[/b]
EDF isn't famous for destroying consoles for no good reason, the horizon will be [b]blanketed[/b] with enemies, and explosions will [b]crush[/b] weaker machines. I tried to play this game on my laptop and if I was lucky I could get into a game, only for it to crash when shit really hit the fan.
[b]MAKE SURE YOU CAN RUN THE GAME AND YOU'LL BE FINE[/b]
I have a GTX780 with 16GB of RAM and consistantly run it at 60FPS.
My buddies who have weaker PCs than me also have consistant frame rates.

[h1]Gameplay (multiplayer)[/h1]
Amazing.
If you have friends willing to play this with you It's pretty much a [b]must buy.[/b]
The weapon variety and synergy between the 4 classes bring about a lot of amazing moments in the multiplayer, and even if everyone wants to play the same class, you can make that work too. The scale is huge, the destructability is reminiscent of Mercenaries 2, and every aspect is just over the top. Ever want to drive a baneblade that gets sent backwards through buildings everytime it fires? Well this game has that and a whole bunch more crazy stuff.
Also the voice acting is hilarious. Every time an NPC says something me and my friends always can't help but snicker.
I should probably also mention that the game is done in "missions" that each can take anywhere from a few minutes to roughly a half hour, giving both plenty of missions for drop in quickplay or long hardfought battles.

[h1]Gameplay (singleplayer)[/h1]
It depends how much you value the style of the game.
If you love crazy B-movie story/voice acting/fights a lot then I would say this game is still worth, even if one of the classes aren't very good for singleplayer (Air Raider). 
However if you're looking for an in-depth third-person shooter with gripping singleplayer then this isn't the game for you, at least not at full price. This game is best played with other people, and there are plenty of pubs.

[h1]Story[/h1]
How much you enjoy the story depends on how much you can appreciate the cheesey style of an alien invasion. The game mixes a lot of cheesey comedy with actual dark themes, such as [spoiler] having everyone die.[/spoiler] Which is a perfect mix for me. However if you want a very dark and edgy story of doom and gloom then this isn't really for you.

[h1]Japanese menus[/h1]
Holy shit the menus are bad.
I'm not kidding, they are by far the only downside to this game. It's very clear the developers are new to PC ports.
You will have to get used to using the arrow keys a fair bit, as they are really the easiest way to navigate the menu screens without considering taking a 9mm asprin.

[h1]Conclusion/TL;DR[/h1]

    [*]Great multiplayer gameplay
    [*]Alright singleplayer
    [*]Charming character and theme that may or may not be for you. (So bad, it's good!)
    [*]Awful menus. Menu autists stay away.

I've been playing the EDF series since the very first game in 2003.
EDF 4.1 is one of the best games ever made when it comes to pure fun, and now it's even better on the PC with a incessant 60 frames per second, a first for the series.

If you're new to the series, here's a quick rundown:
Giant alien insects and robots/aircraft are invading the earth to exterminate all human life.
They are all several magnitudes larger than a tank, and there are an insane number of them. Seriously, there are anywhere between 30 to over 100 enemies in a group at a time.
It's up to you, faceless soldier, to destroy them all. It's essentially B-Movie, the game.

You've got 98 missions, 800 weapons, 4 classes, and 5 difficulties.
About 20 different enemy types including giant ants, spiders, hornets, 30ft tall robots, 50ft tall tripods, and a 300ft tall transformer robot, the Motherships, alien aircraft, and so on.

Don't listen to other people when they say the game is a 'mindless shooter.'
Sure, it can be on the lower difficulties, and that's fine.
But once you try Hardest/Inferno with 4 players online, EDF is far from mindless. Only players with peak reaction speed, communication, situational awareness and tactical planning will succeed.

One word of warning, the first 10 missions of the game are slow and not representative of the whole game.
The progression starts off small with giant ants and boring weapons. 
To really understand what EDF is like, you're likely going to have to play way past the 2-hour refund mark to have access to orbital satellite strikes, fight Godzilla, pilot Pacific Rim Jaegers, use laser snipers, napalm grenades and a whole slew of bad-ass content.
It is well worth it.

EDF is a testament to the fact that most of the time, the simplest games are the best ones.
Nothing since Doom has demonstrated that better than EDF. It's a beloved series, and if you're even slightly interested, you simply owe it to yourself to give it a try.

Like many, I’ve discovered about some great games thanks to Steam. [b]EARTH DEFENSE FORCE 4.1 The Shadow of New Despair[/b] is one of them. When I was a kid, I always dreamed about a game in the same vein as the movie [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tq6pCO3O66I]Empire of the Ants[/url] (1977), which I had watched on TV many, many times during my childhood. I've discovered about the Earth Defense Force (EDF) series last year, and I patiently waited for a good discount, which came recently, with a base price drop as well. And I was blown away to see how much pure fun this game is, and it certainly worth the full price if you like third person shooters, co-op extravaganza (local and online), some mindless action, and don’t mind simple graphics and cheesy presentation. 

EDF is all about having fun. The story is very simple: you must exterminate giant insects that came from space and for some weird reason, there are dragons to fight too and giant mechas to defeat. Yeah, if you’re looking for something that makes sense, look elsewhere, but if you just want to turn off your brain for a while and have fun, EDF is for you. 

While this game offers a great co-op experience, it’s also very fun in single player, and there are even bots to assist you in every level. And while the focus is to fight hundreds of waves of enemies, in the best [i]musou[/i] fashion, sometimes you will have to repeat some previous levels to grind for more powerful weapons and armor, which drops from the enemies. The good news is that it’s a joy to replay levels here, since the mobs have a totally random behavior, so no two levels will play exactly the same, with the level design being the exception. 

EARTH DEFENSE FORCE 4.1 comes with 89 levels, four classes and five difficulty modes. If you enjoy the game enough to replay on all difficulty settings with every class, you will have 1,780 different levels to play, and I mean it, since they feel very different in each difficulty and class. And if you want more, the Mission Pack DLCs offers 49 more levels, but be aware that all achievements are tied to the base gam, so you won’t need any DLC to get all achievements, which is good because you’ll need only the base game, but it’s also bad if you want to 100% the Mission Packs and care about achievements. There’s also a Versus mode, which I haven’t played yet. 

Overall, [b]EARTH DEFENSE FORCE 4.1 The Shadow of New Despair[/b] is a great game for those who value gameplay over graphics and story, but I can see it’s not for everyone. The game starts slow and it gets faster on mission seven, and gladly you can beat all of those in about one hour on Normal (or less on Easy), so you can get to mission eight (where things get really good), and have a good idea of the game before the limit to refund. Personally, I’m having a blast with this game, and I hope you find it as fun as I do.

[b]Cons[/b]:

[h1] Overview [/h1] 

Earth Defense Force 4.1: The Shadow of New Despair, or more commonly referred to as EDF, is a third person shooter that puts you in the shoes of an unnamed soldier of the Earth Defense Force that is tasked with locating and eradicating giant insects and robots from across the globe. Your mission is simple – kill everything that moves.

You’re given four class options before starting: Ranger, Fencer, Wing Diver or Air Raider. Rangers are your typical versatile infantry class, able to equip a variety of guns, sniper rifles, or a plethora of explosives and specialty weapons. Your next option is the Air Raider, a class that has the ability to call in buffs such as shields, turrets, healing modules and heavy armor, such as tanks, helicopters and a slew of different mechanized vehicles. Your third option is the lightly-armored, agile and swift-moving Wing Diver, an all-female crew of airborne infantry that use energy weapons and jetpacks to quickly move about the battlefield. Your final option is the Fencer, EDF’s dual-wielding tank, comprised of thick armor and massive cannons at the expensive of maneuverability. 

The entirety of the game will pit your class of choice and a handful of NPC AI against hordes of insects, robots, dragons and ships as you battle your way through every level. An improved feature over previous installments is the presents of your AI counterparts, which brings a greater feeling of an army, rather than just you versus the world. Some levels lack a sufficient amount at the expense of a higher difficulty, but overall the game doesn’t feel as void of human life as it once did.

There’s not much for plot aside from the simple “save the world” dynamic, set in a cheesy Japanese monster movie environment. I cannot stress this enough: [i] this game is cheesy [/i] and it is meant to be. The dialog is ridiculous, over-the-top and for all accounts just plain goofy, but the game knows that and plays it up all too well. I never felt the game suffered from a lack of plot or bad dialog, as I was far too enthralled with the sheer amount of destruction I was causing in every level to really care.

While progressing through the level, you’re only real task aside from dishing out death while avoiding it yourself is pickups you get from enemies in the realm of armor and weapons. Armor drops increase your overall character’s “armor” rating, which stands in place of a traditional unit health. Weapon drops give you a random chance of finding a new or upgraded version of a weapon you might already have. However, more often-than-not, you might find yourself with two dozen of the same weapons you already own, which can be rather annoying. 

This process of grinding is necessary for higher levels and increased difficulty settings, so expect to replay levels to gather extra armor and weapons so you can tackle particularly tricky levels. During my time playing I never felt that grinding was particularly time consuming, nor did it break the momentum of the game either; EDF is just too damn fun so any issues I ran into didn’t damper my enjoyment at all.

[*] The “cheese” factor – This game is cheesy. The NPC’s dialog, your commanding officer’s, the fact that you can sing while being dead, but it all adds up to a hilarious and amusing time saving the world. That’s just EDF’s inner charm.

I can't believe how good this game is. I laughed at them asking for $50 for about a year, given the dated visuals and lack of presentation...but I finally bit on the $30 sale, and the sheer gameplay depth here is astonshing. Don't be fooled, the game does look like it's straight out of the early X360 days (because it is), the story and voice acting is B-movie at best, and playing this with anything other than a gamepad is essentially lunacy.

But the sheer variety in classes and their loadouts is what kept me in this game. I've never seen another game like this diversify gameplay across four classes so well - you've got a mix of bullet hell and tactical shooter in the Ranger, the Wing Diver is essentially half resource management and half Mercy, the Fencer gets to act like he's either in Armored Core or he's Reinhardt, and the Air Raider gets to call in tactical nukes, mechs, bombing runs, and file paperwork.

Co-op play is a must for this game. Find another person to bring along with you at a minimum - this game is nothing but a disappointment alone. The classes were built to work with each other, and most of them aren't as effective without support in some fashion.

It's not a perfect game by any means - for every great gameplay decision they seem to make a terrible one, and the console port isn't without its flaws. It's a game not meant to be taken wholly seriously, although there is plenty of room for tactical play if you're into it. (Most of my complaints actually stem from the in-game menus and matchmaking - stuff easily overlooked once you're in the thick of it.)

Overall? It's highly worth it if you like the sound of a co-op shooter with depth, lots of explosions, and hilarity. If you're on the edge, get it on sale, but I honestly think the $50 they ask for it isn't out of the question. It's got a lot of polish underneath the dated surface.

This is one of those games that does not run well, but is enjoyable to play. This is even further expanded when considering the tactical options of CO-OP, having your Air Raider provide transport, Riflemen be good consistent mid range damage, airstrikes from Wing Divers and Lancers UFYS (un fracking your stuffing).

How badly does it run? Well, let's just say you can get easly sub 20 fps very easily, regardless of what your rig really is.
My guess is that it bottles up on 2 cores in the CPU for the AI and ignores the rest entirely, but that's just a theory.

The graphics and overall visual presentation is nothing to write home about. Sometimes there are some interesting set pieces, but given the nature of the games mission design, you'll see every environment in then game at least 3 times.

The gameplay can be solid, albeit, somewhat repititive. If you don't play a very mobile class (or don't understand the efficient lancer jump jet reposition mechanic) you feel slow. So slow, that most enemies outrun you on the lowest difficulty setting, which slightly lowers their movement speed.

Some classes are clearly superior to others. Wing Divers for example, have by far the greatest mobility in the game. So much so that they are faster than most of the vehicles the Air Raider can call in.

Lancers are supposed to be the hardest to kill, but their mobility makes it really easy to be a large target.

Riflemen are the "Dark Souls" class of the game. You can role, but don't get invincibility frames when you do so (if you do, there are so few that it doesn't matter). They also give healing to any AI in their squad, but on the higher difficulties this doesn't matter because most of the time, they are dead insanely fast.

Air Raiders can call in powerful support abilities on top of placing upgrades and providing vehicles. They are by far the most useless in direct combat, however, they can give significant damage bonuses, decrease incoming damage, heal and even provide energy for the wing diver.

Getting into CO-OP can be a mess. It's one of those games where you can invite someone in steam, but it only takes them to the main menu. Further invites just make you seem like you're not hosting a lobby.

I would get this game on sale, but I purchased it on sale before the price dropped. I think it was including the sale, around 70% more expensive.

EDF sets you a goal--destroy everything that moves before it kills you--and leaves the rest up to you. It's not open world, but in pure fun factor and "did you see that???" moments it's up there with the likes of Just Cause 2 and Saints Row 3/4.

As Spinal Tap said, there’s a thin line between clever and stupid.

It is not clear which side of the line Earth Defense Force falls, or whether it deftly straddles the line before falling on it’s head. EDF has the beating, unconvincing latex and ketchup heart of a B movie, and every component of the game is below par. The graphics would have been primitive ten years ago, and the animation truly needs to be seen to believed – a jumbled mess of spazzy death animations and clipping errors, assuming the enemies get that far and don’t just vibrate repeatedly against a poorly rendered tree for the whole battle. To the game’s credit, nearly every structure in the game can be destroyed, and the buildings fall apart with all the force, dynamism and realism of a Styrofoam jenga tower.

And yet, it all works. The extraordinary level of jank on display is entirely in keeping with its B-movie inspirations. The terrible voice acting is absolutely spot on in both languages – every actor sounds like they’re reading their lines for the first time with a mixture of confusion and disbelief, and every line has only the most tangential relation to the last. It sounds like a conversation between two concussion victims, and it is glorious.

The game itself has been described as Dynasty Warriors with giant insects, and that’s a pretty on point comparison. Whatever the mission claims to be, you have one objective – kill all the red blobs on the radar. There is a surprisingly excellent variety in enemies, even with the inevitable palette swaps, and despite the jank the controls are responsive and tight. The four classes have admirable variety as well, from the nimble jetpack enabled wingdiver (taking to the air sans breastplate and trousers, ostensibly to reduce weight) to the vehicle summoning support class air raider. There’s a huge variety of weapons available to each class as well, and in co-op building a balanced team is key to survival.

Whether or not I can recommend EDF to you will depend on your circumstances. As a single player, EDF is enjoyable but repetitive and lonely, and the difficulty is very uneven with some enemies being a breeze for one class whilst being a nightmare for others. It’s obviously built for co-op, and this is where it’s manic gameplay shines – getting one shot by a superlaser 90% through a mission is annoying but hilarious when a friend can drive over and revive you, but utterly infuriating in single player. The class based gameplay and ridiculous excess are at their best when enjoyed with inebriated friends, a playable Mystery Science Theatre where the enjoyment comes both because of and in spite of its budget and limitations.

Unfortunately on the PC version at least, the game is plagued by cheating, and cheating players can permanently screw up your save file. The cheating is so ubiquitous that I cannot recommend playing with randoms if this is your only multiplayer avenue. With a friend or three and a suitable level of intoxication/brain damage however, the game is a blast and absolutely worth the surprisingly hefty outlay – but this is not a situation that everyone is lucky enough to be in.

When I was a kid, I had a lot of free time. In between playing Halo, Legend of Zelda, and Oblivion, I spent a good chunk of my time drawing on printer paper. I doodled massively over-the-top stick figure battlefields, featuring chaotic explosions, a large wealth of ridiculous, impossible weaponry, and too many corpses for a young child to be happily doodling. Mind you, none of these drawings were made out of teen angst or a lust for violence. I made them in awe of the badassery I witnessed in games in general. I always wanted to play a game where I could just join that chaos, kinda like throwing action figures at each other over and over again. That is where EDF comes in to save the day.

EDF is a game made for a very specific crowd: a crowd that I find myself zealously a part of. The closest comparison I can think of in modern gaming are those videos where somone goes on top of a mountain in Skyrim, console spawns 50000 cheese wheels, and rolls them down a hill just for the hell of it. Perhaps an even better analogy is that EDF encapsulates the need to have massive battles in games like Fallout 4, but the engine seems to prohibit that by tanking the framerate unless you have a beefy PC. It's a game about that kind of chaos, with a good amount of Starship Troopers spice thrown in. In my mind, it's a neat title about blowing tons of giant insects up with a nuke over and over again.

With all that in mind, EDF isn't perfect. Here are some things that EDF definitely needs to change:

- There is an astounding lack of depth. With "over 800 weapons" as the steam page advertises, I had a very hard time finding weapons that actually provide depth, especially with the Ranger class. The only class that I feel has genuine tactical depth is the Wing Diver, where shooting your gun depletes the same energy meter you use for your jet pack. Other than that, there are a ton of weapons, but most of them are tiered, higher DPS versions of the previous weapon.
- Friendly AI is the epitome of stupid. They simply act as bullet sponges.
- The graphics have not aged very well, seeing as this is a title from 2 console generations ago with updated textures
- Vehicles handle absolutely horrendously, as if the wheels of cars were made of butter, and helicopters turned only in slow motion
- Classes like Air Raider, a vehicle support class, end up getting squashed on harder difficulties due to their dependence on delayed vehicle drops
- The Ranger is almost universally good, its only downside being that it can't fly like a Wing Diver

In my opinion, this isn't a game you (the consumer) should go into expecting to find a great story, or meet great characters (or any characters for that matter). EDF is purely about the chaos of the fight, and I believe that is where it shines the brightest. With 80's B-Movie humor everywhere in this game, it's hard to take seriously, but that's probably a good thing. Now I'd like to discuss things that make EDF worthy of my recommendation:

+ I never had any issues with framerate, no matter how many enemies were on screen
+ That being said, there are a LOT of enemies on screen. Battles span miles across maps, with hundreds upon hundreds of active participants
+ Split screen co-op is an absolute riot, assuming you have a spare gamepad
+ Sound design is solid, with explosions sounding particularly fun
+ The soundtrack is catchy as all hell
+ The "EDF Chant" that the little soldiers do in the game is both adorable and hilarious, adding a lot to the game's humor
+ Difficult as all hell, especially on the "Inferno" difficulty and in the DLC expansion packs
+ Tons of missions with a good amount of reply value
+ Finding new weapons has an aura of satisfaction, providing reasons to keep playing the game
+ Oozing with Japanese sci-fi charm, often referencing old science fiction in the process
+ 4 classes with their own uses, allowing for a multitude of playstyles
+ Despite a wealth of samey weapons, some are genuinely creative and unique to the series as a whole, like the Limpet guns

As a complete package, EDF 4.1 is worth the 50 dollars, assuming you want a game like this. It's not a very tactically deep game, but it's got 50 dollars worth of explosions, giant insects, and alien armies to at least keep the average player entertained. When stripped down to its bare matter, EDF is a game about throwing a bunch of action figures at each other, or creating massive battlefields, or just seeing what happens when you nuke 500 giant bees. And to me, that's a game well worth its hefty price tag.

Pretty mixed thoughts on EDF 4.1, I was looking forward to playing an EDF game, especially after I'd heard so much about the series being the "best worst games ever" and with 4.1 being a more preferred by many over 5, I picked this one up. Do I hate it? No, I don't hate it. Sadly however I found it a lot less user-friendly and developed than I'd have liked, I'm not enjoying it and don't feel I'm getting anywhere so can't justify continuing to play it. I've got a lot of thoughts on why I felt this way so to try and keep this more simple, I'll put the issues I had down to three factors:

[u]Controls[/u]
I found it to be pretty clunky, I ended up rolling around at 45 degree angles as the Ranger for example as there isn't a sprint or the ability to roll forward. Playing the Fencer, the heavily-armed tanky unit, was satisfying until I realised that there isn't really much fun when you want to get somewhere, you can thrust forward a bit over and over but nothing more. It just ends up feeling bothersome. You'll also end up using weapons strangely too, aiming assault rifles at unusual angles because "it fires that way", it's plain silly... Accuracy may increase with the "level" but why should a weapon be so bad by default? It makes some of them It's practically unusable unless you're willing to aim wrong.

[u]User Interface/Experience[/u]
The interface is strange, there isn't a cursor so you end up clicking to select and using WSAD to move around the menus, menus that don't always feel intuitive. Every time you start the game you'll be notified with a popup "You will use the mouse" etc., it's badly translated and shouldn't even be a message you need to see. Things like that add up.

[u]Progression[/u]
Now this is the seriously disappointing surprise to me... It may have been the dealbreaker. I suspect it also is to anyone that values upgrade systems and customisation. There's no real armour upgrades, visual or functional, just an number that goes up that's essentially just health. Aside from that one health value, you also won't have any kind of progression with your character, no stats, no skills, nothing. What you will get are guns, guns that only level-up when "looted" again, that's it. I feel like a lot of depth is lost here, it could be so much more. Oh and sure, you can change two colours on your uniform but that's hardly of much value. It'd be nice to at least have several armour sets with different stats for each class. It would nice to have [i]something[/i] to feel like you're progressing yourself and not just random weapons.

So, in summary, things just don't sit right for me here, especially from a game that was released on PC in 2016. As someone that's played a lot of games, this one feels like it offers something grand but forgets to give you the full suite of tools to embrace it. A strange experience.

These days, it feels as if the game industry has been split between massive, multi-morbillion dollar titans and smaller, shorter independent ventures, with very little in the middle. The 7th generation of consoles ushered forth the HD era of gaming, which meant that developing games would cost way more than it ever had before. Because of this, AA Devs and publishers who didn't have the biggest budgets could no longer turn out the more varied games with little investment as they had prior. Each game was more costly, and each failure was more dire. Many shifted focus to the Nintendo Wii, the last major Standard Definition console with a huge install base, but by the time the 8th generation of consoles hit the market, many of these AA devs and publishers had bit the bullet (notable examples being Midway and THQ).

Yet, despite the odds, Sandlot and D3 Publisher have endured.

Earth Defense Force (EDF) has been going strong since it's humble origins as a Simple Series game back in 2003. These were low budget games with sold for 2000 yen, and EDF (alongside Onechanbara) got it's start here before becoming the cult hit it is today. The first two games never came stateside, but the third entry in the series "Earth Defense Force 2017" did back in 2007 as an Xbox 360 exclusive, and I believe it's where most longtime fans in this part of the world first experienced the series. I remember picking up a used copy when I was 8 or 9 in one of those used game bins at a Blockbuster near my house that we'd visit if the Hollywood Video literally right across the street didn't have anything good for sale. I think I just picked it because I saw bugs on the cover (which was the same reason I picked up Escape From Bug Island), but I am really glad that I did.

When I got back home, I popped the game in and was CONSUMED by it's fun, stupid bullshit for hours and I have been still for 15 years and multiple games! All EDF games are basically the same, you kill everything that moves in impressively massive maps set in various locals across Japan (or abroad in EDF2). It's really simple, but the game offers so many tools to murder these massive ants, spiders, mechs, kaiju, etc that it rarely (if ever) got dull. The games' charm stem from it's almost 1950's throwback vibes (the game's premise is an amalgamation of THEM, War of the Worlds and Gojira, and a fair few of the music tracks being played on a Theremin) and it's over-the-top-ness. You level entire skylines in your quest to murder all the alien bastards who've invaded earth as your team mates shout the most ridiculous lines put to a script and it's just so fucking fun! Tell me, how many games can you order helicopters to air drop and multi-story high rock-em-sosck-em robot to fist fight (LEGALLY DISTINCT) Godzilla as your buddies call in air strikes to tactically nuke thousands of bugs in the middle of Tokyo?

I love these games, I love that many others have come to love them as I have, and I love that they are still able to make them despite the odds!

This game is gloriously imperfect.  The imperfections are obvious before you're too far into the game.  An enemy or two won't even enter the zone and you'll have to give up occasionally.  The art is sufficient.  The acting is (intentionally) B movie schlock.  But here's why you play: because no other game has you outnumbered 200-to-1 as you grit your way through them with a mix of gumption and alien doodads.  Every time you do it, you get more toys to play with, more levels to play in, and an opportunity for yet more ridiculous setups.  Plus you get showered with havoc-physics giant insect parts.  It's a wild ride, and any gamer who says they like action needs to play this game.

A fun little arcade-style shoot 'em up with four different classes to choose from and a LOT of missions to play, with five different difficulty settings too!

Can get a bit tedious because of the grind that is getting higher Armor values and better gear, since enemies have a chance to drop the following on death:
- Armor crate
- Weapons crate
- Small healthkit
- Large healthkit

Since you have to collect all these crates by touching them, having to go around the level to get your hands on these will take a lot of time (Armor and Weapons drops also only apply to the class you are playing so you have to go through the same song and dance if you want to play another class)
And this grind is mandatory if you want to play on higher difficulties and not get your ass handed to you.
You can balance this out by playing with friends but you'll inevitably reach a mission that is effectively impossible because you don't have high enough gear to be able to deal with all the shit that's coming at you!

But with that in mind, I would still recommend this game if you want a dumb little shoot 'em up where you gun down entire hordes and legions of giant bugs and alien invaders in the name of a globalist defense organization.
